title: Negative Electronic Energy and the Zero of Energy
topicTitle: Postulates of Bohr's atomic model and its application
notes: Why Bohr energies are negative, what the zero of energy means, and the three energy relations (E, KE, PE) that follow from the force condition.
### Where the negative sign comes from

Bohr takes the zero of energy at infinite separation — the electron just free of the atom, at rest. Any bound orbit is *below* that reference, so all bound-state energies are negative: $E_{n}=-13.6\,Z^{2}/n^{2}$ eV. The magnitude |E| is the binding energy — exactly the energy that must be supplied to free the electron (ionisation).

From the Coulomb force condition, $\frac{mv^{2}}{r}=\frac{kZe^{2}}{r^{2}}$ gives $KE=\frac{kZe^{2}}{2r}$ and $PE=-\frac{kZe^{2}}{r}$. Therefore: **KE = −E** and **PE = 2E = −2|E|**, with E = KE + PE. Check for hydrogen ground state: E = −13.6 eV, KE = +13.6 eV, PE = −27.2 eV. As n grows: E → 0⁻, KE → 0, PE → 0⁻ (a loosely bound, slow electron).
• n = 1: E = −13.6 eV (most tightly bound, v = c/137).
• n = 2: E = −3.4 eV; n = 3: −1.51 eV; n = 4: −0.85 eV — level differences shrink as 1/n², hence the converging spectral series.
• n = ∞: E = 0 — ionisation; the electron is free.
### Why the sign matters in chemistry

Ionisation energy = |Eₙ| (positive number supplied); electron affinity and bond energies follow the same convention (energy *released* on going to a bound state is positive when reported as 'released'). Mixing the two sign conventions is the standard source of error — always state which convention you use.
confusion: ❌ Negative energy means the calculation is wrong. ✅ It is a *bound state* referenced to infinite separation.
❌ KE is also negative. ✅ KE = −E is positive (½mv²); only total E and PE are negative.
❌ The electron loses mass when bound. ✅ Mass–energy differences are negligible here (13.6 eV vs 511 keV rest mass).

universalFacts: Hydrogen ground state: E = −13.6 eV, KE = +13.6 eV, PE = −27.2 eV.
The virial theorem for Coulomb systems (2KE + PE = 0) is the general reason behind PE = 2E.
IE of hydrogen in molar units is 1312 kJ mol⁻¹ — the value measured calorimetrically.
examples: **Problem:** Photon energy to move H from n = 2 to n = ∞? **Solution:** 0 − (−3.4) = 3.4 eV — the second ionisation step of the excited atom; the photon must supply at least 3.4 eV (λ ≈ 364.6 nm, the Balmer limit).

summary: All bound-state energies in Bohr's model are negative because the zero of energy is chosen at infinite separation — the electron just free of the atom, at rest. Any permitted orbit lies below that reference, so Eₙ = −13.6 Z²/n² eV, and the magnitude |Eₙ| is the binding energy, exactly the energy needed for ionisation. The force condition gives the three relations used in every numerical: KE = kZe²/2r, PE = −kZe²/r, and therefore KE = −Eₙ and PE = 2Eₙ, with Eₙ = KE + PE. For the hydrogen ground state E = −13.6 eV, KE = +13.6 eV and PE = −27.2 eV, a general case of the virial theorem 2KE + PE = 0 for Coulomb systems. As n grows, E → 0⁻, KE → 0 and PE → 0⁻, which is why the level spacing shrinks and spectral series converge.
importantConcepts: Zero of energy at infinite separation, so every bound orbit has Eₙ = −13.6 Z²/n² eV
|Eₙ| is the binding energy and equals the ionisation energy 13.6 Z²/n² eV for that level
From the force condition: KE = kZe²/2r and PE = −kZe²/r, hence KE = −Eₙ and PE = 2Eₙ
Virial theorem for Coulomb systems: 2KE + PE = 0, the general reason behind PE = 2E
Sign conventions in chemistry: ionisation energy is reported positive, Eₙ stays negative
importantStatements: A bound electron has negative energy; a negative sign indicates a bound state, not an error.
For hydrogen in its ground state E = −13.6 eV, KE = +13.6 eV and PE = −27.2 eV.
Kinetic energy is always positive (½mv²); only the total energy and the potential energy are negative.
As n → ∞, Eₙ → 0, KE → 0 and PE → 0⁻, so the electron becomes free and the level spacing vanishes.
The mass–energy change on binding (13.6 eV) is negligible beside the 511 keV electron rest energy.

keyPoints: Zero of energy = infinite separation; bound states lie below it.
KE = −E and PE = 2E are the two relations every Bohr numerical needs.
Hydrogen ground state: −13.6 eV total, +13.6 eV kinetic, −27.2 eV potential.
IE of hydrogen in molar units is 1312 kJ mol⁻¹ — the experimentally measured value.
specialNotes: Mixing the 'energy released' and 'energy absorbed' sign conventions is the standard source of error; always state which you use.
PE is twice the total energy, not half — the ratio comes from the inverse-square force, not from arithmetic.
As levels crowd towards zero, the series limit corresponds to the ionisation threshold (Balmer limit 364.6 nm).
